A.explanation: Acceleration describes rate of change of velocity, so $g$ appears, but its definition does not link force through a distance to energy.

B.explanation: Momentum is $mass \times velocity$ and is conserved in collisions, but it does not give energy gained by lifting through $\Delta h$.

C.explanation: Power is the rate of energy transfer with time, but time does not appear in $\Delta E_P = mg\Delta h$.

D.explanation: Work done is defined as force times displacement in the direction of the force, so $mg \times \Delta h$ gives the energy stored as $\Delta E_P$.

hints: Notice the mass $m$ is raised through vertical height $\Delta h$, so an upward force equal to the weight $mg$ acts over that distance.
Recall which quantity is defined by a force $F$ acting through a displacement $s$ in the direction of the force as $F \times s$.
Compare $\Delta E_P = mg\Delta h$ with the form (weight) x (vertical distance) to see which listed definition produces stored energy.
walkthrough: Identify the situation: to raise mass $m$ at steady speed, the upward lifting force must balance the weight $mg$ downwards over the vertical displacement $\Delta h$.
State the physical rule: work done $W$ is defined as the force times the displacement in the direction of the force, $W = Fs$.
Apply the definition to the lift: $F = mg$ and $s = \Delta h$ in the same upward direction, so the work done by the lifting force is $W = mg\Delta h$.
Link work to energy: this work transfers energy to the object and is stored as the gain in gravitational potential energy, so $\Delta E_P = W = mg\Delta h$.
Therefore the derivation needs the definition of work done. This is option D.
